t: The Tocharians are known by a borrowed name: scholars called their languages after the Tókharoi of Bactria, an identification now generally considered erroneous, and what they called themselves is unknown.
Their two languages, Tocharian A and Tocharian B, were Indo-European, and by glotto-chronological data closest to Western branches such as proto-Germanic and proto-Italic.

Their oasis cities, Kucha the largest, were Buddhist centres on the Silk Road; they never recovered from the Tang conquest of the 640s, and their people blended with the Uyghurs, whose language replaced theirs.
dyk: Among the everyday texts written in Tocharian are travel passes: small slips of poplar wood telling the officials at the next station along the road the size of the caravan allowed to pass.
ev: Settled Bronze Age farming communities appear in the oases of the northern Tarim and the Turpan Depression
The Xiongnu drive the Yuezhi from western Gansu and then overcome the Tarim statelets
After campaigns begun in 108 BCE, the Han dynasty establishes the Protectorate of the Western Regions under Zheng Ji
Kumārajīva of Kucha, captured in 384, is brought to Chang’an, where he heads a translation bureau until his death in 413
The Hephthalites rule the region, and the swordsmen of the Kizil Caves appear to have been painted in these years
The monk Xuanzang visits Kucha and records about a hundred convents with more than five thousand monks
The Tang send an army under Ashina She’er, who takes Kucha and later has 11,000 of its people executed in reprisal for the killing of the protector-general
The Tocharian languages die out as the oasis peoples blend with the Uyghurs, who found the Kingdom of Qocho in 866

f.homeland: The oases of the northern Tarim Basin and the Turpan Depression (modern Xinjiang, China): Kucha (Kuśi), the largest, Agni (Yanqi, Karashar) and Turpan with Qocho (Gaochang); the Kizil Caves 65 km west of Kucha; perhaps also Krorän on the southeast edge of the basin.
f.period: Farming communities in the oases from c. 2000 BCE, before the Tocharian languages are attested; city-states by the 2nd century BCE, listed in the Book of Han; under the Xiongnu, the Han, the Rouran, the Hephthalites (c. 480–550), the Turks (from c. 560) and the Tang (from the 630s–640s); the languages believed extinct during the 9th century.
f.known: the Tocharian A and B languages, written in a variant of the Brahmi script; Buddhist monasteries of the Sarvāstivāda school; the murals of the Kizil Caves; the monk and translator Kumārajīva of Kucha; oasis cities on the northern Silk Road; travel passes on slips of poplar wood; one love poem in Tocharian B
f.sources: Some 7,600 manuscripts recovered from about 30 sites in the northeast Tarim from the early 20th century, named “Tocharian” by Friedrich W. K. Müller; Chinese histories (the Book of Han, the Book of Jin) and Xuanzang’s Records of the Western Regions; the Kizil murals; studies of the Tarim mummies and ancient DNA.
